chunks: Nyquist rate and why it matters. The question: What is the nyquist rate of a signal? Why is it important?
The Nyquist rate is the minimum rate at which you must sample a signal without losing information. It is twice the signal's highest frequency.
Sampling makes copies of the signal's spectrum (its list of frequencies), repeated at multiples of the sample rate.
If you sample fast enough, the copies stay apart and you can recover the original. If you sample too slowly, they overlap and high frequencies masquerade as low ones.
That is aliasing, and it cannot be undone afterward.
Imagine pressing the same rubber stamp repeatedly along a strip of paper at fixed spacing. The stamp is your signal's spectrum, and the spacing is the sample rate.
If the stamp is narrower than the spacing, each print stands clear. If the stamp is wider, neighboring prints overlap and smudge.
Once smudged, you cannot tell which ink came from which print.
In (a) the signal bandwidth B is less than half of f s, so the original (centered at 0, shown for positive and negative frequency) and its replicas at f s, 2f s do not touch.
In (b) B exceeds f s/2; the red regions are where replicas overlap, so frequencies above f s/2 land on top of frequencies below it.
The dashed line marks the Nyquist frequency f s/2.
Bandwidth: the range of frequencies a signal contains, for most signals from zero up to its highest frequency.
Nyquist rate: twice the signal's highest frequency, a property of the signal. Nyquist frequency: half the sample rate you actually use, a property of the sampler.
Aliasing: frequencies folding into lower ones. Anti-alias filter: a filter before the sampler that removes content above the Nyquist frequency.
Oversampling: sampling much faster than the Nyquist rate.
Audio with content up to 20 kilohertz has a Nyquist rate of 40 kS/s. A converter running at 48 kS/s has a Nyquist frequency of 24 kilohertz. CD audio samples at 44.

"The Nyquist rate is twice the signal's highest frequency, the minimum sample rate that preserves it: 40 kS/s for 20 kilohertz audio.
The Nyquist frequency is half your actual sample rate.

It matters because sampling replicates the spectrum around multiples of fs; above 2B the copies don't overlap and you can reconstruct perfectly, below it high frequencies fold down as aliasing and can't be recovered.
That's why you need an anti-alias filter and sample somewhat above Nyquist."
